summary: Malta is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (ETIAS is not yet in operation), and everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa handled through Malta's Central Visa Unit and its visa centers abroad.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

source.instrument: Regulation (EU) 2018/1806, Article 4(1) — stays of no more than 90 days in any 180-day period

fee.notes: Children 6–11: €45; under 6: free. Fee set EU-wide since June 11, 2024.

source.name: Visa Code (Regulation (EC) No 810/2009), consolidated text — EUR-Lex
source.instrument: Regulation (EC) No 810/2009 establishing a Community Code on Visas, Article 16(1) (visa fee) and Article 1(1) (stays not exceeding 90 days in any 180-day period), consolidated to 11 June 2024

fee.notes: For stays over 90 days: work, study and other long-stay purposes, usually alongside a residence-permit application. Confirm the current fee and requirements with Identità or the Maltese mission before applying.

source.name: Identità — Central Visa Unit, applicable fees
source.instrument: Long-stay Visa Fees Regulations, 2020 (L.N. 287 of 2020), regulation 1(2) (validity not exceeding 365 days) and Schedule (EUR 100 for any purpose other than study)

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Malta entry requirements

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.certificate: International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis (ICVP)
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required from travelers aged nine months and over arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission, including those who spent more than 12 hours in transit through such a country's airport.

source.name: WHO, International Travel and Health, Annex 1 — countries requiring proof of vaccination against yellow fever
source.instrument: International Health Regulations (2005), Article 36 and Annex 7; WHO International Travel and Health, Annex 1, 18 November 2022 (revised 3 January 2023)

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it but border officers may ask about cover.

source.name: Visa Code (Regulation (EC) No 810/2009), consolidated text — EUR-Lex

declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border. There is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorization System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travelers will need an ETIAS travel authorization to enter the Schengen Area. It is not yet in operation, and no applications are being collected; the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. Check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU (EU rules): 200 cigarettes (or 100 cigarillos, 50 cigars or 250 g of tobacco); 4 liters of still wine and 16 liters of beer, plus 1 liter of spirits or 2 liters of fortified or sparkling wine; and other goods worth up to €300, or €430 arriving by air or sea.
Between EU countries, goods bought for your own use with taxes paid are not taxed again; customs can ask you to show that larger quantities are not for resale.

payments.text: No official source describes how widely cards are accepted in Malta. The UK Foreign Office advises caution when exchanging money and using ATMs, and avoiding carrying large amounts of cash where possible.

safety.text: Malta is very safe with low violent crime. Watch for pickpocketing in Valletta and on crowded buses, and take the usual care in the Paceville nightlife district late at night.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Malta?
faq.answer: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely. US, UK, Canadian, Japanese and around 60 other visa-exempt nationalities can stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period across the Schengen Area (ETIAS is not yet in operation). Everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa, handled by Malta's Central Visa Unit through its missions and visa centers.

faq.question: How much does a Malta Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa costs €90 for adults and €45 for children aged 6–11, allowing up to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries. National long-stay (Type D) visas cost around €100. Confirm with the Maltese mission.

faq.question: Is ETIAS required to enter Malta?
faq.answer: ETIAS for visa-exempt travelers across the Schengen Area is not yet in operation, and no applications are being collected; the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. Once mandatory, the €20 online authorization will be required before boarding. Check the official EU website for the current status.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Malta without a visa?
faq.answer: Visa-exempt non-EU visitors can stay up to 90 days within any 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area, so time spent in Italy or any other Schengen country counts toward the same limit. EU and EFTA citizens can stay indefinitely but should register if settling for more than 3 months.

faq.question: Do Gozo and Comino need separate arrangements?
faq.answer: No — Gozo and Comino are part of Malta, so whatever lets you enter Malta covers the whole archipelago.
